questions.question: Which sentence is a more polite way to ask for information?
questions.explanation: We often use phrases like 'Can you tell me...' or 'Do you know...' to make questions more polite. These are called indirect questions.

correct: Do you know where I can buy a spade?

correct: Can you tell me how far the bus station is?

content.passage: To keep healthy, it is important to follow some basic rules. First, a balanced diet is essential. This means eating a variety of foods, including fruits which are full of vitamins, and avoiding too many fats. Second, regular exercise helps keep your body fit and strong. Third, good hygiene can prevent the spread of diseases. For example, cleaning a small injury with disinfectant can stop an infection from developing. For more serious illnesses like the flu, rest is important. Sometimes, a doctor might give you a prescription for tablets to help you recover. Finally, prevention is key. For diseases like cholera, it is crucial to be immunized, especially when traveling. Following this advice can help you avoid getting sick and needing a doctor.

activities.title: Read the Story: Barry Jones - London schoolboy
activities.instruction: Reading time! 📖 Read carefully and the story about Barry's bad morning. Then answer the questions to check your understanding.
activities.compensates: Replaces teacher-led reading of PB page 6 and gist questions.

content.passage:
'Come on, Sue. Give me the cornflakes. I'm late.'
'Say please,' said Sue, giggling.
'Please,' I said. 'And hurry up! It's half past eight!'
'Dad can take you in his taxi,' said Sue.
'No, he can't. He's gone,' I said.
'Do you want an egg, dear?' shouted Mum from the kitchen.
'No thanks, Mum. I'm late.'
Sue giggled again and I wanted to know why.
'What are you laughing at?'
'Nothing,' said Sue and giggled for the third time.
Sue was just thirteen, about two years younger than me, and sometimes I could not understand her.

Ten minutes later, I was sitting upstairs on the bus with my Geography textbook open on my knee. There was a test in the first period.
'Hi, Barry,' somebody said behind me. It was my friend, Kevin. We had been at Central Comprehensive School for almost five years. I turned round and Kevin laughed. 'Your face!' he said. 'It's all black. Don't you wash?'
'Sue!' I shouted. She had put some trick soap in the bathroom before I went in. My face had got dirtier instead of cleaner.

The bus stopped. We flew downstairs and I ran to the school washroom. Then I ran to the Geography lesson.
'I'm sorry I'm late, sir,' I panted.
'I'm sorry too,' said Mr Edwards, our Geography teacher. 'Sit down and do the test.'

'Where's that soap, Sue?' I asked when I got home. She didn't answer.
'Anne's coming,' she said.
'Who's Anne?' I asked.
'She's my pen-friend from France,' said Sue. 'She's coming to stay next week - for a month.'

lessons.description: Practice Type 1 and Type 2 conditional sentences
objectives: Use Type 1 conditionals for likely situations
Use Type 2 conditionals for unlikely situations

activities.title: Conditional Sentences
activities.instruction: Learn about the two types of conditional sentences.

content.passage:
Type 1 Conditionals:
When a condition is likely to be fulfilled, the result is likely to happen.
Structure: If + present simple, ... will + verb
Example: If I work hard, I will pass the exam.

Type 2 Conditionals:
When a condition is not likely or impossible, the result is not likely to happen.
Structure: If + past simple, ... would + verb
Example: If I had a helicopter, I would fly over the mountains.
